title: Filtered crystals require an essential-image condition

Colmez and Fontaine identify weakly admissible filtered \((\varphi,N)\)-modules with semistable \(p\)-adic representations, providing a precise later comparison for part of this programme (Colmez & Fontaine, 2000, Theorem A and §4). The sheet states no weak-admissibility condition and gives only a semilinear operator in its filtered-crystal description, so one must distinguish the crystalline specialization from the broader semistable theorem. That theorem does not establish all six proposed descriptions or classify arbitrary geometric motives.

title: The precise scope of Oda’s comparison
body:
**Kind:** unpursued implication

**Context search:** `Dieudonné | p^A | extension` → Adds a local-field programme to CT54/007 and CN D05; the supplied Oda PDF, Corollary 5.11, printed p. 131, supplies a characteristic-p realization comparison.  
**Results ledger:** MPL_14_002-044 M24a [first-pass lead; rational abelian-realization background]; WG2 §2.4 #3 [unchecked plan; broad motives connection, not an established period result]

Oda’s Corollary 5.11 canonically compares the Dieudonné module of the \(p\)-torsion of an abelian variety over a perfect field of characteristic \(p\) with \(H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}\), compatibly with the Hodge exact sequence (Oda, 1969, p. 131). This gives a precise comparison behind the question in CT54/007, while the local lift, the rational \(p\)-adic representation and the essential image proposed in 18/005 remain additional problems.

title: Recovering the cyclotomic kernel requires a hypothesis
body:
**Kind:** unproved claim  
**Witness:** `18/006:L35–45`  
**Brief quotation:** \(\operatorname{Ker}u\) … connu  
**Context search:** `Tate | cyclot | Kummer | Ker` → Adds a comparison of two splittings to CT16/052, which gives an analytic Kummer generator, and CT44/008, which uses twisted Tate modules; neither supplies this kernel equality.  
**Results ledger:** MPL_14_002-044 B04 [first-pass lead; weights and cyclotomic characters]; WG2 §2.4 #3 [unchecked plan; broad motives connection, not an established period result]

The formula \(\varphi(\gamma)=u(\gamma)j_2(\chi(\gamma))^{-1}\) immediately gives \(\varphi=u\) on \(\ker\chi\), but the displayed equality \(\ker u=\ker\chi\cap\ker\varphi\) also requires \(\ker u\subseteq\ker\chi\). A sufficient structural reason would be that the Tate character \(\chi\) factors through the realization \(u\); this condition must be checked before using the asserted quotient and its induced character.

title: An index problem in the associated-graded twist
body:
**Kind:** reading question  
**Witness:** `18/009:L2,8–21`  
**Brief quotation:** Twist de Tate sur structures de Hodge mixtes  
**Context search:** `Tate | poids | graduation` → Adds mixed-Hodge twist conventions to CT16/003–006, which treats gradings and projectors, and CT44/008, which uses Tate twists; neither gives this associated-graded formula.  
**Results ledger:** LM7 C.1 [Known, the return’s claim; integral weights of one 1-motive]; MPL_14_002-044 B04 [first-pass lead; weights and Tate conventions]

The general convention \(W_i(E(n))=W_{i+2n}(E)\), \(F^i(E(n))=F^{i+n}(E)\) agrees with a Tate twist of weight \(-2n\) (Deligne, 1971, §2.1.13). Under that convention the associated-graded identity is \(\operatorname{Gr}_i^W(E(-1))\simeq(\operatorname{Gr}_{i-2}^W E)(-1)\), whereas frozen line 14 retains unshifted indices and an incomplete parenthesis; this interpretation belongs in the note and must not replace the recorded formula.

To justify the assertion one must identify the tensor filtrations of fixed type with these homogeneous spaces and construct the relative unipotent group acting on the splitting space; the existence of splittings for individual filtered vector spaces is insufficient.

This is an interpretation question; the frozen symbols remain unchanged.

title: The explicit strong period conjecture
body:
**Kind:** conjecture  
**Witness:** `18/011:L65–76`  
**Brief quotation:** Conj. de transcendance forte; alors ?  
**Context search:** `transcend | period | torseur` → Adds the written witness requested in context/README.md; CT16/021 concerns the transcendental part of H², CT16/035 concerns Bott periodicity, and CT47/003 has unrelated torsors, with no corresponding period conjecture.  
**Results ledger:** WG2 §2.4 #3 [unchecked plan; broad motives connection, not an established period result]; no dedicated period-conjecture entry

For \(k\subset\overline{\mathbf Q}\), the sheet asks whether \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k k(\alpha,\beta)=g+u\), where \(g=\dim G\) and \(u=\dim U^{\prime}\). The intended equality contains maximal transcendence of the Betti–de Rham comparison \(\alpha\) and an additional independence assertion for the Hodge-splitting comparison \(\beta\), making it stronger than the ordinary period equality \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k k(\mathrm{periods})=\dim G\) (Bost & Charles, 2016, §2.2).

For \(k\subset\overline{\mathbf Q}\), applying additivity in the other towers, with the displayed quotient bounds, yields the intended dimensions \(g-b\) and \(g-\ell\) without providing evidence for the initial strong conjecture. Confidence is high for this conditional calculation because transcendence degree is additive in towers, but only medium for its application here until the two descriptions of \(Q\) are reconciled.

The further assertion that one point \(g\) generates \(G\), under semisimplicity and transcendence of \(\pi\), needs an argument controlling the central torus and the normalization; the displayed dimensions alone do not supply it.

title: Schneider’s theorem does not establish the proposed equality
body:
**Kind:** unproved claim  
**Witness:** `18/012:L13–22`  
**Brief quotation:** Contient le th. de Schneider  
**Context search:** `Schneider | ellip | transcend` → Adds a proposed transcendence consequence absent from the supplied context; CT54/003, 005 gives an abelian de Rham comparison but no Schneider theorem or period-independence claim.  
**Results ledger:** WG2 §2.4 #3 [unchecked plan; broad motives connection, not an established period result]

The cancelled claim of transcendence degree \(3\) for four normalized elliptic periods, with determinant \(1\) as the only relation, is substantially stronger than transcendence of individual periods or the classical CM criterion for an algebraic period ratio. Grothendieck’s published note distinguishes Schneider’s theorem from conjectural algebraic independence of periods and quasiperiods, so the manuscript’s phrase cannot serve as a proof of the displayed degree (Grothendieck, 1966, p. 102, note 10).

The cancelled draft adds \(j\) to the normalized period tuple and predicts total transcendence degree \(4\), while the margin raises a special algebraic-\(\tau\) case and contains a deleted question about \(\pi\) over \(k\). Modern André–Grothendieck formulations count the transcendence of the ground field together with that of the periods through an inequality over \(\mathbf Q\); this is a comparison of formulations, not an identification of the uncertain “pré-minimal” condition or a proof of the manuscript’s equality (Bakker & Tsimerman, 2025, Conjecture 1.2).

The live sheet distinguishes the non-CM \(\mathrm{GL}_2\) case, predicting degree \(4\), from the CM torus case, predicting degree \(2\). In the modern torsor formulation this is the corresponding Grothendieck period conjecture; the CM elliptic case is known, while the full non-CM degree-\(4\) assertion does not follow from the weaker de Rham–Betti results cited here (Bost & Charles, 2016, §2.2).

title: Generation of the elliptic period locus is weaker than genericity
body:
**Kind:** conjecture  
**Witness:** `18/013:L8–10`  
**Brief quotation:** A-t-on \(H=G\)  
**Context search:** `torseur | groupe engendré | ellip` → Adds a separate weaker period question absent from CT47/003, whose torsors concern integral transforms, and CT16/049, whose subject is motivic semisimplicity.  
**Results ledger:** WG2 §2.4 #3 [unchecked plan; broad motives connection, not an established period result]

Choose a \(\overline{\mathbf Q}\)-point of the period locus and translate that locus to contain the identity; the smallest algebraic subgroup containing the translate describes the smallest algebraic torsor generated by the period point. For one elliptic curve, the coefficient-field theorem of Kreutz et al. (2026, Proposition 3.1 and Theorem 5.13(ii), arXiv v3) supplies an affirmative modern comparison after this torsor identification is made precise. This does not establish that the original period locus is itself the full torsor, or prove the non-CM transcendence degree \(4\).

title: The Hodge-splitting question matches Katz’s later question
body:
**Kind:** conjecture  
**Witness:** `18/013:L12`  
**Brief quotation:** Peut-on avoir \(h\in\overline Q\)  
**Context search:** `Hodge | extension | splitting` → Adds arithmetic transcendence of the analytic splitting to the de Rham extension in CT54/003, 005 and its discussion in CN D01–D02.

For a non-CM elliptic curve over \(\overline{\mathbf Q}\), the sheet asks whether its analytic Hodge splitting can descend to algebraic coefficients. Katz asks whether an elliptic curve over a number field whose Hodge decomposition is defined over algebraic coefficients must have CM (Katz, 1976, Question 4.0.8, p. 501). This is a close later literature witness; the sources checked here establish neither a claim of priority nor a current resolution of that converse.

title: The CM margin has an eigenspace proof
body:

After adjoining the CM endomorphisms and their eigenvalues, a non-scalar CM endomorphism acts on \(H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}\) with two distinct algebraic eigenlines whose complexifications are \(H^{1,0}\) and \(H^{0,1}\). Katz gives this argument explicitly, verifying the CM direction after the necessary extension of the field of definition (Katz, 1976, Lemma 4.0.7, p. 501).

These missing definitions prevent turning the cancelled formula into a fully specified theorem statement and leave the diplomatic alternatives intact.

The one-dimensional residue calculation gives \(P_{\mathrm{an}}=2\pi i\,P_{\mathrm{top}}\) for the chosen orientation, and multiplicativity predicts the codimension-\(p\) factor \((2\pi i)^p\). This agrees with retaining Tate factors in Betti–de Rham comparison, but the local integral does not verify every supported-cohomology map in the global diagram (Deligne, 1982, §1).

The frozen \(X^{\prime\,n-p}\) may use an unstated convention or be a draft slip; dimension counting raises the question without permitting a silent substitution of \(p\).

body:

title: The orientation choice has an exact Tate-line map

title: The displayed natural isomorphism has a minus-minus tensor defect
body:
**Kind:** own idea (explicit calculation). **Witness:** 18/035:L9–24. **Quote:** “n'est pas compatible avec le produit tensoriel”. **Context search:** `foncteur | Betti | tordu | tensor` → PN A06/A23 (15/199–201,215), CT16/049; adds a complete calculation of the displayed map. **RS:** MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 A06, A23. **Confidence:** high; reason: multiplication of the two explicit scalars gives the defect.

For \(W(V)=V^+\oplus iV^-\), the map \(a_V(v_++v_-)=v_++iv_-\) is a Q-linear isomorphism, and ambient multiplication gives the tensor comparison \(W(V)\otimes W(U)\to W(V\otimes U)\). For \(v\in V^-\) and \(u\in U^-\), that multiplication sends \(a_V(v)\otimes a_U(u)\) to \(-v\otimes u\), whereas \(a_{V\otimes U}(v\otimes u)=v\otimes u\). The calculation proves the particular map's failure and also shows why the subspace W itself remains closed under the required tensor construction.

title: The tentative tensor nonisomorphism is detected on an Artin line
body:
**Kind:** own idea (explicit obstruction). **Witness:** 18/035:L26; 037:L20. **Quote:** “Il semble”. **Context search:** `tordu | cocycle | real | frobenius` → PN A23 (15/215), CT16/049; adds an explicit obstruction on a tensor subcategory. **RS:** MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 A23; WG2 §2.4 #3. **Confidence:** high; reason: the tensor relation yields an impossible rational square.

Let A be the sign Artin motive of C/R, with Betti basis a, \(a\otimes a\mapsto1\), and \(f_\infty(a)=-a\); then \(W(A)=i\mathbf Q a\), whose tensor square maps \((ia)\otimes(ia)\) to −1. Any tensor isomorphism between the two rational fibre functors on the Artin subcategory would send a to \(qia\), with \(q\in\mathbf Q^\times\), and preservation of \(A^{\otimes2}\simeq\mathbf1\) would give \(-q^2=1\), an impossibility. This proves the obstruction for the full real-motive category containing A; on the Tate subcategory the explicit maps \(e_n\mapsto i^n e_n\) on \(\mathbf Q(-n)\) preserve tensor products, so the manuscript's category scope matters.

title: The cohomology-of-real-points line needs its superscript resolved
body:

For these tests, \(X(\mathbf R)\) means the usual R-rational points, equivalently the fixed locus of complex conjugation: for \(X=\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf R}\), \(H^1(X(\mathbf C),\mathbf Q)^{f_\infty}=0\), whereas \(X(\mathbf R)=\mathbf RP^1\simeq S^1\) has \(H^1=\mathbf Q\). Scan040 instead writes the quotient \(X(\mathbf C)/\pi\), which for this example is a closed disk and has the rational cohomology of the invariant part. The degree-zero reading also requires care: for \(X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C\) over R, there are no real points but the invariants in the two-point complex Betti H⁰ equal Q. These calculations leave the frozen `*|0` unchanged and make the superscript and the intended fixed-locus-versus-quotient convention questions for a future reading, rather than assigning the usual rational-point meaning to the manuscript without examination.

On the Tate category, the real comparison torsor has group \(\mathbf G_m\), and the real lines in the two fibre functors admit a tensor-compatible isomorphism chosen on their generator. Its cocycle value −1 is the explicit coboundary \(i^{-1}\bar i=-1\), but the distinguished period comparison is imaginary in the generator convention of scan029. Thus the equation on scan036 correctly tests \(\alpha\in P(\mathbf R)\); replacing that test by the existence of some point of \(P(\mathbf R)\) changes the assertion even in this example.

title: The even-Tate converse fails on the Artin–Tate summand
note_kind: own idea (verified counterexample to the written assertion)
body:
**Kind:** own idea (verified counterexample to the written assertion). **Witness:** 18/036:L21–29; 038:L16. **Quote:** “somme de puissances tensorielles de Q(2)”. **Context search:** `Q(2) | frobenius | Tate | tordu` → PN A23/M03 (15/215;18/011), plus RS's Hua entry; adds a complete realization of the lead's counterexample. **RS:** Hua, findings register, **18-real-frobenius-trivial-converse**; MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 A23, M03. **Confidence:** high; reason: algebraic projectors and two eigenvalue computations suffice.

For the sign Artin motive A and \(T=\mathbf Q(-1)\), the actual motive \(L=A\otimes T\) has \(f_\infty=(-1)(-1)=+1\), yet its Hodge weight is 2. It occurs as the anti-invariant summand for the algebraic deck involution on \(H^2(\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf C})\), with \(\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf C}\) regarded as an R-scheme, whereas tensor powers of \(\mathbf Q(2)\) have weights in \(4\mathbf Z\) and direct summands preserve the weight grading. The computation supports Hua's recorded refutation and remains valid in this Artin–Tate example with algebraic Hodge classes, so the page's “moyennant conj. de Hodge” does not remove it; Appendix A supplies the projector.

title: The abstract group Gm does not determine real Frobenius
body:
**Kind:** own idea (explicit comparison). **Witness:** 18/036 diagram. **Quote:** “G ≃ Gm ou G ≃ {e}”. **Context search:** `Tate | hom central | graduation | G_m` → PN M03/M11/P14 (18/011–012); adds a test of the displayed vertical equivalence. **RS:** MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 M03, M11, P14; LM1 A.8 remains its supplied “Refuted, return's claim”. **Confidence:** high; reason: the two rank-one characters generate faithful one-dimensional groups with opposite specified involutions.

The subcategory generated by T has group \(\mathbf G_m\) and real Frobenius −1, while the subcategory generated by \(L=A\otimes T\) has group \(\mathbf G_m\) and real Frobenius +1. In each case every nonzero tensor power has nonzero weight, so there is no relation killing a power of its generating character; arbitrary invertible scalars therefore give the Tannaka group. The exact quotient characters from \(\mu_2\times\mathbf G_m\) are \(\rho_T(a,t)=t\) and \(\rho_L(a,t)=at\); they send the same specified involution \((-1,-1)\) to −1 and +1, proving that these two identifications with the abstract group \(\mathbf G_m\) do not identify its distinguished real Frobenius.

title: The final totally-real-field assertion has an embedding calculation
note_kind: own idea (explicit verification of the stated intersection)
body:
**Kind:** own idea (explicit verification of the stated intersection). **Witness:** 18/041:L20–26. **Quote:** “Kr est une ext. algébrique”. **Context search:** `tot.*réel | totally real | K_r | topologie` → PN A12 (15/207) records a different totally-real-extension question; no matching intersection formula found in CT. **RS:** MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 A05 and WG2 §2.4 #3 are broad links; no dedicated settled row. **Confidence:** high for the field calculation over all archimedean embeddings; reason: extension of a transcendence basis constructs the required embedding.

For the manuscript's K admitting an archimedean embedding, any transcendental \(t\in K\) can be included in a transcendence basis and sent to a nonreal transcendental complex number, after which the embedding extends over the remaining algebraic extension into C. The induced topology has complex completion, because its image contains \(\mathbf Q+\mathbf Q\sigma(t)\), a dense subspace of C, so t is excluded from the intersection of the written \(R_T\). An algebraic element survives exactly when each of its conjugates is real, since each embedding of its number field extends to K; consequently the intersection is precisely K's totally real algebraic subfield.

title: Polarization and real Frobenius meet in the positive Weil form
body:
**Kind:** own idea (explicit compatibility calculation). **Witness:** 18/034 normalizer formula; 037; 038 cancelled normalizers. **Quote:** “f∞ j(λ) f∞⁻¹ = j(λ′)”. **Context search:** `polarisation | positive | autodualité | Hodge` → CT44/002,008–009 and PN B03 (15/203,215,217); adds the morphism and sign calculation connecting the two structures. **RS:** MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 B03; WG2 §2.3 #12; MPL_14_002-044 A36 retains first-pass status. **Confidence:** high; reason: functoriality of the polarization and \(C^2=(-1)^n\) give the identity.

On a weight-n geometric realization equipped with a specified polarization morphism over R \(q:V\otimes V\to\mathbf Q(-n)\), functoriality gives \(q(fx,fy)=(-1)^nq(x,y)\). With the Weil operator C, the live normalizer relation gives \(fCf^{-1}=C^{-1}\), and the positive real form \(B(x,y)=(2\pi i)^nq(x,Cy)\) satisfies \(B(fx,fy)=B(x,y)\) by the two cancelling signs. Appendix C records the exact calculation; this is the requested bridge through an actual pairing and involution, with no assertion that the involution alone chooses a polarization.

title: The nonlinear real-section map has a precise linear image
body:
**Kind:** unpursued implication. **Witness:** 18/034,037 real Frobenius; 039–040 real descent. **Quote:** “automorphisme ... x↦x̄”. **Context search:** `réellification | real structure | section | polarisation` → PN B03 (15/203,215,217); adds the abelianization map relating the real-section comparison to this manuscript's involution. **RS:** MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 B03; LM7 E.23 remains Open and is not resolved by this comparison.

For a smooth projective hyperbolic curve over R, Pál's real-section result identifies \(\pi_0(X(\mathbf R))\) with conjugacy classes of continuous sections of its arithmetic fundamental-group sequence. A section sends complex conjugation to a lift whose conjugation action on the geometric group descends through \(\pi_1(X_{\mathbf C})\to\pi_1(X_{\mathbf C})^{\rm ab}\), and dual étale H¹ realizes the corresponding real Frobenius. Two lifts differ by an element of the geometric group, whose inner action vanishes after this abelianization; consequently this conjugation action on the abelianization retains the involution while forgetting the possible component distinction recorded by the section class; this calculation does not discard the section cocycle from the entire abelianized extension.

title: The product-of-elliptic-curves dimension count is explicit
body:

The coordinate map $(A,A',t)\mapsto(A[1:0],A'[1:0])$ to $\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf P^1$ has stabilizer the two upper triangular determinant-one groups and the scalar factor, giving the displayed dimensions $3+3+1=7$ and $2+2+1=5$. The uncertain opening non-isogeny condition is preserved as a reading question and cannot be silently replaced by a standard hypothesis.

title: The relative-position quotient accounts for the bound (n−1)d
body:

The page uses $P_i=\underline{\operatorname{Isom}}(\xi,\xi_{v_i})$ and the diagonal action on their product. This provides the explicit morphism behind the author's numerical improvement from $(n-1)m^2$; the interpretation of an adelic “point's transcendence degree” still needs a chosen component or a precise coordinate-algebra definition.

title: The literal products leave a topology question
body:

\[
{}^\tau\varphi(\sigma)\varphi(\tau)

The morphism $D_g:x\mapsto x^{-1}g$ is an algebraic isomorphism over $k$ with inverse $y\mapsto gy^{-1}$ and carries the automorphism orbit of $g$ to the image of this $\varphi$. \[
j(E_t)=1728\frac{4(-3t/(t-1728))^3}{4(-3t/(t-1728))^3+27(-2t/(t-1728))^2}=t.
\]

At $t=\pi$ the curve has a field of definition of transcendence degree one, and every field of definition contains its transcendental j-invariant, while $\pi$ is already algebraic over $k_0=\mathbf Q(i,\pi)$. This is a curve-level test of the base-field qualification: applying its minimum to the manuscript's motive $M$, including $h^1(E_t)$, still requires an isogeny/descent argument, which the $j$-calculation does not supply. title: The partial-inverse lowering operator has an explicit rational conversion to the \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) lowering operator

body:
**Kind:** own idea (explicit calculation) attached to a prior context question. **Witness:** 18/027, \(H^2(\mathbf P^1)=\mathbf Z(-1)\), provides a new elementary test object; the relevant operator formulas are CT16/013–014 and 033. **Context search:** `Lambda | sl_2 | Lefschetz | projecteurs` → CT16/013–018,033; PN M02, R01; RS WG2 §2.3 #2. **RS:** WG2 §2.3 #2, §2.4 #3 [unchecked]; PN M02 [lead]. **Relation:** supplies the conversion map needed before transporting the \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) terminology. **Confidence:** high; reason: direct commutator calculations on every string basis vector.

On the explicit primitive string \(v_j=L^jv\), \(0\leq j\leq m\), put \(E(v_j)=v_{j+1}\), \(\Lambda(v_j)=v_{j-1}\), \(F(v_j)=j(m-j+1)v_{j-1}\), and \(H(v_j)=(2j-m)v_j\), with $E(v_m)=0$ and $\Lambda(v_0)=F(v_0)=0$. Direct subtraction gives \([E,F]=H\), \([H,E]=2E\) and \([H,F]=-2F\), while \(F=\sum_{j\geq1}j(m-j+1)\Lambda\pi_j\) and \(\Lambda=\sum_{j\geq1}[j(m-j+1)]^{-1}F\pi_j\) over \(\mathbf Q\). CT's displayed endpoint-projector identities are therefore related to the conventional \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) matrices by these coefficients; the transcription's separate contraction-model formulas and its integral assertions still require their own normalization check.

title: The two rational operator images have explicit matrix units
body:
**Kind:** own idea, explicit calculation. **Witness:** CT16/013–018,033; current 18/027. **Quote:** “ξ(Z(−1))” on 18/027. **Context search:** the `Lambda | sl_2 | Lefschetz | projecteurs` search recorded for MB03, CT16/013–018,033 and PN M02/R01; separately repeated for MB03b in `context_searches.jsonl`. **RS:** WG2 §2.3 #2, §2.4 #3 [unchecked]; PN M02 [lead]. **Relation:** verifies the rational operator-image comparison through actual maps. **Confidence:** high, from the matrix units and Casimir eigenvalues displayed below.

On the model \(W=\bigoplus_{m=0}^d V_m\), where \(V_m\) has the displayed string basis, write \(B=1-E\Lambda\) and \(T=1-\Lambda E\); then \(B_m=B\Lambda^mTE^mB\) projects precisely onto the bottom vector of the length-\(m\) string. The operators \(E^bB_m\Lambda^a\), \(0\leq a,b\leq m\), are its matrix units, proving \(\mathbf Q[E,\Lambda]\cong\prod_{m=0}^d\operatorname{Mat}_{m+1}(\mathbf Q)\) by direct action on the basis. For the \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) image, \(C=H^2+2H+4FE\) acts on \(V_m\) as \(m(m+2)\), so polynomial interpolation in \(C\) projects onto each \(V_m\) and interpolation in \(H\) projects onto each \(v_j\); the formulas above recover \(\Lambda\) and the same matrix units from \(E,F,H\). These are the explicit morphisms identifying the two rational operator images, with multiplicity spaces carried by identity operators in the exterior-algebra model; no integral equality is inferred from divisions by \(j(m-j+1)\).

title: \(\mathbf P^1\) gives both the failed factorization and the surviving relation
note_kind: own idea (explicit calculation) / explicit calculation, sharpening an already registered example
body:
**Kind:** own idea (explicit calculation) / explicit calculation, sharpening an already registered example. **Witness:** 18/027, “\(\xi(\mathbf Z(-1))\)”. **Context search:** `P^1 | Lefschetz | SL_2 | Tate` → CT16/017; PN M02; RS MPL_14_087-132 M04. **RS:** MPL_14_087-132 M04 [first-pass own-idea lead]; WG2 §2.4 #3 [unchecked]. **Relation:** restates the \(\mathbf P^1\) test with matrices and a normalization action, rather than claiming categorical separation. **Confidence:** high; reason: the displayed matrices and their action on the unit vector.

In \(V=\mathbf Qe_0\oplus\mathbf Qe_2=H^*(\mathbf P^1)\), \(E=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(F=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(H=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\), whereas the pure Tate category generated by \(\mathbf Q(-1)\) has group \(\mathbf G_m\) acting as \(\rho(z)=\operatorname{diag}(1,z)\). Every \(\rho(z)\) fixes \(e_0\), and the displayed Lefschetz \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) action moves \(e_0\), proving that this particular representation does not factor through \(\rho(\mathbf G_m)\). The relation is explicit nonetheless: \(\rho(z)E\rho(z)^{-1}=zE\), \(\rho(z)F\rho(z)^{-1}=z^{-1}F\), and the correspondence \(E:h^0\to h^2(1)\) is equivariant after its Tate twist.

The tensor grading has \(w_{M\otimes N}=w_M\otimes w_N\) and \(w_{\mathbf Q(1)}(t)=t^{-2}\), the central grading described by [DM, Definition 5.1]. For \(\varepsilon\) equal to the character on \(\mathbf Q(-1)\), \(\varepsilon\circ w=t^2\), whereas PN's earlier 18/011 records \(\varepsilon\circ j=\mathrm{id}\); this exponent calculation is the comparison needed before identifying the two maps, and the Levi-to-full-group lift remains unspecified there.

title: The Hom comparison has a common number-field base and an abelianization morphism

Faltings's Satz 4 identifies \(\operatorname{End}_K(A)\otimes\mathbf Z_\ell\) with \(\operatorname{End}_{G_K}(T_\ell A)\) for a number field \(K\); the off-diagonal block of \(A=J_X\times J_Y\) gives the corresponding Hom map [F83], while Tate's original main theorem treats finite fields [T66]. For smooth proper geometrically connected curves $X,Y$ of genus at least two over the same number field $K$, a morphism \(f:X\to Y\) induces \(\pi_1(f)\), whose geometric pro-\(\ell\) abelianization is \(T_\ell(f_*):T_\ell J_X\to T_\ell J_Y\); this is the exact route from the fundamental-group Hom data to the abelian-variety Hom data. Mochizuki's Theorem A reconstructs dominant morphisms from the prescribed open homomorphisms of arithmetic fundamental groups modulo geometric inner automorphisms over sub-\(p\)-adic fields, including number fields [M99].

For \(\mathbf G_m\), every rational representation is a direct sum of characters, while conjugation \(\mathbf G_m\to\operatorname{Inn}(\mathbf G_m)\) is the trivial map with kernel \(Z(\mathbf G_m)=\mathbf G_m\). For the hyperbolic geometric fundamental group \(\Delta\) in Mochizuki's setting, Lemma 1.3.1 and Corollary 1.3.2 identify \(\Delta\) with \(\operatorname{Inn}(\Delta)\) and recover \(\Pi\) as the pullback \(G_K\times_{\operatorname{Out}(\Delta)}\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)\) [M04]. Thus the useful relationship is the sequence \(1\to Z(G)\to G\to\operatorname{Inn}(G)\to1\): the Tate example computes its kernel explicitly, and the anabelian reconstruction uses the zero-kernel case.

**Kind:** self-flagged / admitted lemma. **Witness:** 18/049, lemma; 18/051, opening and margin. **Quote/state:** “si on admet ceci”; “Donc en admettant ce lemme”. **Linked observations:** P07, P08. **Context search:** `approximation|renforc|compact|générique` → PN P33, 18/006; no matching lemma in CT. Adds the componentwise-generic-coset step; PN P06/A06 and WG2 §2.4 #3 [leads/plan].

title: 18/051, approximation argument
body:
